n: The Lord gently tells Samuel to stop mourning for Saul and move forward. He sends Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint a new king from Jesse's sons. God is already providing.

f.g: An animal horn used as a container for anointing oil.

n: Samuel fears Saul will kill him for anointing a rival. The Lord tells him to bring a heifer and go to offer a sacrifice — a true purpose that also protects him.
Samuel is to invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and the Lord will show him which son to anoint. Samuel must rely on revelation step by step.

f.w: him whom I name unto thee

n: When Samuel arrives, Bethlehem's elders tremble and ask if he comes in peace. A visit from the prophet could mean judgment.
Samuel reassures them and tells them to purify themselves for the sacrifice. He personally prepares Jesse and his sons.

f.g: Prepare through ritual washing and purification.

n: Samuel sees Eliab, the oldest — probably tall and impressive like Saul — and assumes he must be the Lord's choice.
The Lord corrects even His prophet: don't judge by looks or height. People see the outside, but the Lord sees the heart. One of scripture's most important teachings.

f.w: the LORD looketh on the heart

n: Jesse brings his second son, Abinadab, but the Lord has not chosen him either.
Next comes Shammah, the third son, but again the Lord says no.
Seven sons pass before Samuel, and none is chosen. Seven often signals completeness, yet God's choice is outside the expected group.
Samuel asks if these are all. Jesse mentions the youngest, out tending sheep — so overlooked he wasn't even invited. Samuel insists they wait for him.

f.g: A shepherd would become Israel's shepherd-king.

n: David arrives — healthy, with bright eyes and a handsome look — and the Lord says, “Arise, anoint him: this is he.”

f.g: reddish, with a healthy glow; perhaps reddish-haired

n: Samuel anoints David among his brothers, and the Spirit of the Lord rests on David from that day on. This is the first time David is named in the book.
The Spirit leaves Saul, and a troubling spirit torments him. The Joseph Smith Translation clarifies that this evil spirit was not from the Lord.

f.w: an evil spirit from the LORD
f.g: JST: “an evil spirit which was not of the Lord.” The Hebrew can also mean a harmful or distressing spirit.

n: Saul's servants notice his torment and recognize it as spiritual in nature.
They suggest finding a skilled harpist whose music could bring relief when the troubling spirit came. Music has a real power to calm and lift the spirit.

f.g: A lyre (Hebrew kinnor), a small stringed instrument.

n: Saul agrees and asks them to find a good musician.
One servant recommends a son of Jesse: skilled in music, brave, wise in speech, handsome, and — most importantly — the Lord is with him.
Saul sends for David, “who is with the sheep.” Ironically, the rejected king invites his anointed replacement into his own court.
Jesse sends David with gifts for the king — bread, wine, and a young goat — as was customary.
David enters Saul's service, and Saul loves him and makes him one of his armor-bearers. This love will soon turn to jealousy.
Saul asks Jesse to let David stay permanently in his service because he is so pleased with him.
Whenever the troubling spirit came on Saul, David played the lyre, and Saul would feel refreshed and the spirit would leave.

f.w: the evil spirit departed from him
f.g: JST: an evil spirit “which was not of God.”
